goals: Write the valence configurations of the s-block and p-block groups

slides.heading: s- and p-Block Elements
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the general plan of the s-block and p-block, then groups 1 and 2. **This chapter is formative assessment only:** it is not part of the annual theory paper, but it is taught here at textbook depth for school tests.

visual.alt: Table of the four blocks of the periodic table with groups and valence configurations

slides.narration: Welcome to a short chapter on the s block and the p block. These two blocks hold most of the elements you meet daily: the sodium in salt, the calcium in bones, the aluminium in foil, the carbon in pencils. This chapter is for formative assessment only, so it will not appear in the annual theory paper, but your school tests can ask it. Part one covers general trends and then groups one and two.

slides.heading: Valence configurations of the s-block and p-block
slides.body_md: The s-block fills an **ns** subshell; the p-block fills **np** after ns². Every group has the same valence configuration all the way down, so the **properties follow a pattern within the group**.

visual.alt: Table of s-block and p-block groups with valence configuration, family name and common ions

slides.narration: The s block is made of groups one and two. Their atoms end in an s subshell: one electron in group one, two in group two. The p block is groups thirteen to eighteen, where p electrons are added after the filled s subshell. All members of a group share the same valence shell pattern, which is why they behave alike. The first member of each group is usually the odd one out.

slides.heading: Trends down a group: radius and ionisation enthalpy
slides.body_md: Down a group each atom has **one more shell**, so radius rises; the outer electron feels a weaker pull, so **ionisation enthalpy falls**. A cation is smaller than its atom, because it has lost its outer shell and has the same nuclear charge holding fewer electrons.

visual.alt: Table of atomic radius, ionic radius and first ionisation enthalpy for the alkali metals

slides.narration: Going down group one, every atom adds a whole new shell. So the radius climbs from lithium to caesium. The outer electron is farther from the nucleus and better screened, so it is easier to remove, and ionisation enthalpy falls. The ions are much smaller than their atoms, because losing the outer shell leaves the same nuclear charge pulling on fewer electrons in a smaller cloud. Look at the numbers in the table.

slides.heading: Group 1 trends as plots
slides.body_md: Both curves are smooth: the radius rises and the first ionisation enthalpy falls from Li to Cs. The M⁺ ion is always smaller than the atom.

slides.heading: Ionisation enthalpy in groups 1 and 2
slides.body_md: Group 2 atoms have a **higher IE₁** than their group 1 neighbours (greater nuclear charge, smaller size, filled ns²). But the **second** ionisation enthalpy is huge for group 1 (an inner shell is attacked) and moderate for group 2, so they form **M⁺** and **M²⁺** respectively.

visual.alt: Table of first and second ionisation enthalpies of sodium, magnesium, beryllium, calcium and barium

slides.narration: Compare sodium and magnesium. Magnesium has the higher first ionisation enthalpy because its nucleus carries one more charge and its atom is smaller. But look at the second one. For sodium the second electron comes from a filled inner shell and costs a huge amount, so sodium stops at plus one. For magnesium the second electron is still in the outer shell, so a plus two ion forms readily and its lattice energy pays for the extra cost.

slides.heading: Worked example: why Na⁺ but Mg²⁺?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Using IE₁ and IE₂ (kJ mol⁻¹): Na 496, 4562; Mg 737, 1450. Explain why sodium forms $\ce{Na+}$ and magnesium forms $\ce{Mg^2+}$ in compounds.

**Step 1.** Ratio IE₂/IE₁: Na $= 4562 \div 496 = 9.2$; Mg $= 1450 \div 737 = 1.97$.

**Step 2.** For Na the second electron comes from the **inner 2p shell** (neon core); the jump is about nine-fold, which no lattice enthalpy can repay.

**Step 3.** For Mg the second electron is the other 3s electron; the cost is only about twice IE₁, and the lattice enthalpy of $\ce{MgCl2}$ more than compensates.

**Answer:** Na⁺ (noble-gas core intact) and Mg²⁺ (both ns electrons lost).

visual.alt: Table comparing the ratio of second to first ionisation enthalpy for sodium and magnesium

slides.narration: Work through it in steps. First, divide the second ionisation enthalpy by the first. For sodium the ratio is about nine point two, a huge jump. For magnesium it is only about one point nine seven. Second, ask where the next electron comes from. In sodium it comes from the neon core, so it is costly. In magnesium it is the second outer electron. So sodium forms a one plus ion and magnesium a two plus ion.

slides.heading: Flame colours
slides.body_md: In a flame, heat excites the outer electron of Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Ca, Sr and Ba to a higher level; on falling back it **emits visible light** of a characteristic wavelength. The low ionisation enthalpy makes this easy. **Be and Mg** have small atoms with tightly held electrons, so the flame cannot excite them: **no colour**.

visual.alt: Table of flame colours of alkali and alkaline earth metals

slides.narration: A flame test is a quick way to spot a metal. The heat lifts an outer electron to a higher level. When it drops back it gives out light of one particular colour. Sodium gives golden yellow, potassium violet, lithium crimson red, calcium brick red, strontium crimson and barium apple green. Beryllium and magnesium show no colour, because their electrons are held so tightly that an ordinary flame cannot excite them.

slides.heading: Hydration enthalpy of the alkali metal ions
slides.body_md: A smaller ion has a **higher charge density** and attracts more water molecules, so Li⁺ has the **most negative hydration enthalpy**. The magnitude falls steadily to Cs⁺. Hydrated Li⁺ is therefore the biggest ion in water and moves slowest.

slides.narration: This bar chart shows how much energy is released when each gaseous ion is surrounded by water. Lithium, the smallest ion, has a very high charge density, so it grips many water molecules tightly and releases the most energy. The bars shrink steadily toward caesium. A lithium ion drags a thick shell of water along, so in solution it is the bulkiest alkali ion and conducts least.

slides.heading: Reducing character
slides.body_md: All s-block metals are strong reducing agents (they lose electrons easily); in water the strength is set by IE, sublimation and **hydration enthalpy**. **Li has the most negative E°** of the alkali metals although it has the highest IE₁, because its hydration enthalpy is so large.

visual.alt: Table of standard electrode potentials of selected alkali and alkaline earth metals

slides.narration: Reducing character means how readily a metal gives up electrons in water. Sodium and potassium follow the ionisation trend, but lithium has the most negative electrode potential of all, minus three point zero five volts. Its first ionisation enthalpy is the highest in group one, yet its very high hydration enthalpy more than makes up for that. In group two the reducing power rises from beryllium to barium. All of them are strong reducing agents.

slides.heading: Lithium: the unique first element of group 1
slides.body_md: Li is small, with a high charge density and polarising power, so its compounds show more **covalent character** and it differs from the rest.

rows: Not deliquescent; no hydrate in NaCl or KCl

visual.alt: Table comparing lithium with sodium to caesium in oxide, nitride, nitrate, carbonate, hydrogencarbonate and chloride behaviour

slides.narration: Lithium behaves differently from its group. In air it gives a simple oxide, not a peroxide. It is the only alkali metal to react with nitrogen, forming lithium nitride. Its nitrate breaks down to the oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen, while the others give a nitrite and oxygen. Its carbonate decomposes on heating, and it has no solid hydrogencarbonate. All this comes from its small size and high polarising power.

slides.heading: Diagonal relationships
slides.body_md: Li resembles Mg, Be resembles Al, B resembles Si. Across a period size falls and charge rises; down a group size rises; **diagonally the two effects roughly cancel**, so ions have similar size or charge-to-radius ratio.

slides.narration: Here is the periodic table fragment with the diagonal pairs. Lithium resembles magnesium, beryllium resembles aluminium, and boron resembles silicon. Moving across a period the atoms shrink and carry more charge. Moving down a group they grow. Along a diagonal these effects nearly cancel, so the ions have similar size or similar charge per radius, and the chemistry looks alike.

slides.heading: Worked example: beryllium, the odd one out of group 2
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give four ways in which Be differs from the rest of group 2 and two ways in which it resembles Al.

**Differences:** (1) smallest atom, highest IE₁ (899 kJ mol⁻¹) and highest electronegativity (1.5): **covalent compounds**; (2) **no d orbitals**, so maximum covalency 4 (the others reach 6); (3) BeO and Be(OH)₂ are **amphoteric**; (4) Be does not give a flame colour and resists water.

**Resemblance to Al:** (i) both are rendered passive by concentrated nitric acid; (ii) both dissolve in alkali: $\ce{Be + 2OH- + 2H2O -> Be(OH)4^2- + H2}$.

**Answer:** small size and high charge density explain every point.

visual.alt: Table comparing beryllium with the other group 2 metals and with aluminium

slides.narration: Beryllium is the odd one out of group two for several reasons: it is tiny, it has the highest ionisation enthalpy and electronegativity, so its compounds are covalent. It has no d orbitals, so it can bond to at most four groups. Its oxide is amphoteric, and it dissolves in alkali to give hydrogen. These points are shared with aluminium, as the table shows. Both are made passive by concentrated nitric acid.

Lithium and beryllium are the unusual first members, and they resemble magnesium and aluminium through the diagonal relationship.

slides.body_md: Part 2 — the p-block elements B, Al, Ga, In, Tl and C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb. As in Part 1, this chapter is **formative assessment only** and is taught at textbook depth for school tests.

visual.alt: Table of some elements of groups 13 and 14 with valence configuration and uses

slides.narration: Part two takes us to the p block: the boron family in group thirteen and the carbon family in group fourteen. You meet them as borax in glass, aluminium in foil, carbon in diamond and pencil lead, silicon in sand and chips, and lead in batteries. As in part one this is for formative assessment only. Watch two ideas as we go: the first member of each group is unusual, and heavier elements prefer the lower oxidation state.

slides.heading: Group 13: configuration and data
slides.body_md: Valence configuration **ns² np¹**. The metallic character increases from B (a metalloid) to Tl, but the data are **irregular** because of the poor shielding by inner d electrons from Ga onwards.

visual.alt: Table of atomic radius, M three plus radius, first ionisation enthalpy and electronegativity for boron to thallium

slides.narration: Group thirteen atoms have the configuration s two p one. Look at the table. The radius rises from boron to aluminium, but gallium is slightly smaller than aluminium. Gallium comes after the ten d block elements, whose d electrons shield the nucleus poorly, so the outer electrons feel a stronger pull. The same effect makes the ionisation enthalpies irregular, and electronegativity rises from aluminium to thallium.

slides.heading: Group 13 trends as plots
slides.body_md: Unlike group 1, **Ga < Al in size**, and IE₁ rises again at Ga and at Tl. Cause: the ten 3d electrons (and, for Tl, the 4f electrons) shield the extra nuclear charge **poorly**.

slides.narration: The plot shows the irregularity clearly. The blue radius line dips at gallium, and the green ionisation line goes up at gallium and again at thallium. Inner d electrons and, in thallium, f electrons screen the growing nuclear charge poorly, so the outer electrons are held more strongly than a simple trend would predict. This is the opposite of the smooth behaviour of group one.

slides.heading: Oxidation states and the inert pair effect
slides.body_md: Group 13 shows **+3** (all three valence electrons) and **+1** (only the np electron). Going down, the **ns² pair becomes reluctant to take part**: this is the **inert pair effect**. Al is almost always +3, but **Tl⁺ is more stable than Tl³⁺**.

visual.alt: Table of the stability of the plus three and plus one oxidation states in group 13

slides.narration: Group thirteen elements can lose all three outer electrons to show plus three, or lose only the p electron to show plus one. Down the group the s pair is held more tightly, because the heavy nucleus is poorly shielded and the s electrons are close to it. This is the inert pair effect. Aluminium is almost always plus three, but thallium plus one is more stable than thallium plus three, which is actually a good oxidising agent.

slides.heading: Worked example: energy cost of M³⁺
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Using IE₁, IE₂, IE₃ in kJ mol⁻¹ (B: 801, 2427, 3659; Al: 577, 1816, 2744; Tl: 589, 1971, 2878), find the total energy to form the gaseous M³⁺ ion and comment.

**Boron:** $801 + 2427 + 3659 = 6887$ kJ mol⁻¹.

**Aluminium:** $577 + 1816 + 2744 = 5137$ kJ mol⁻¹.

**Thallium:** $589 + 1971 + 2878 = 5438$ kJ mol⁻¹.

**Comment.** B's huge sum (> 6800) cannot be repaid by lattice or hydration enthalpy, so boron forms **covalent compounds**. Tl's sum exceeds Al's, yet its larger size gives weaker bonds, so Tl³⁺ compounds do not repay the cost: Tl(I) is preferred.

rows: Al³⁺ in ionic and hydrated forms

visual.alt: Table of the sum of first three ionisation enthalpies for boron, aluminium and thallium

slides.narration: Let us add up the cost of removing three electrons. For boron it is six thousand eight hundred eighty seven kilojoules per mole, far too much for any ionic bonding to repay, so boron makes covalent bonds. For aluminium it is five thousand one hundred thirty seven, which hydration and lattice energy can repay. Thallium costs more than aluminium and its bonds are weaker, so thallium usually stays plus one.

slides.heading: Anomalous behaviour of boron
slides.body_md: Boron is a **non-metal**, small, with high ionisation enthalpy and electronegativity, and it has **no d orbitals**, so its maximum covalency is **4**. Its compounds are covalent and **electron-deficient** (BCl₃ has only six electrons around B), so they act as **Lewis acids**.

visual.alt: Table comparing boron and aluminium in nature, oxide, covalency, halide and ions

slides.narration: Boron differs sharply from the rest of its group. It is a non-metal, its oxide is acidic, and its compounds are covalent. With no d orbitals its covalency stops at four, as in the tetrafluoroborate ion. Boron trichloride has only six electrons around boron, so it eagerly accepts a lone pair and is a Lewis acid. Aluminium, by contrast, is a metal with an amphoteric oxide and can reach a covalency of six.

slides.heading: Group 14: configuration and data
slides.body_md: Valence configuration **ns² np²**. Metallic character increases from C and Si (non-metal, metalloid) to Sn and Pb (metals). Covalent radius rises, IE₁ falls (with the small break at Pb), and electronegativity is almost constant from Si to Pb.

slides.narration: In group fourteen the valence configuration is s two p two. Going down, the covalent radius grows and the first ionisation enthalpy falls, though lead is slightly higher than tin. Electronegativity drops sharply from carbon to silicon and then hardly changes. Carbon and silicon are non metal and metalloid, germanium is a metalloid, and tin and lead are metals, so the group shows the whole range of character.

slides.heading: Catenation in group 14
slides.body_md: **Catenation** is the self-linking of atoms into chains and rings. **Carbon** is best at it, because the C–C bond is strong (348 kJ mol⁻¹) and almost as strong as C–H and C–O. The E–E bond weakens down the group, so Si, Ge and Sn form only short chains.

slides.narration: Catenation means atoms joining themselves in long chains and rings. Carbon is the champion. The carbon carbon bond is strong, and its strength is close to that of carbon hydrogen and carbon oxygen bonds, so long chains do not fall apart in the presence of water or air. Down the group the self bond becomes weaker, from silicon through germanium to tin, so those elements only form short chains.

slides.narration: Quick check. Think about bond strengths.

slides.heading: Inert pair effect in group 14
slides.body_md: Group 14 shows **+4** and **+2**. Going down, +2 becomes more stable: **Sn(II) is a reducing agent**, **Pb(IV) is an oxidising agent**, and **Pb(II) is the stable state of lead**.

rows: Sn²⁺ is a good reducing agent
Pb⁴⁺ (PbO₂) is a strong oxidising agent

visual.alt: Table of the stable oxidation states of group 14 elements and the behaviour of the other state

slides.narration: Group fourteen can show plus four or plus two. Carbon, silicon and germanium prefer plus four. Going down, the pair of s electrons becomes inert, so plus two grows more stable. Tin two is a good reducing agent and is easily oxidised to tin four. Lead four is a strong oxidising agent: lead dioxide oxidises hydrochloric acid to chlorine, and lead two is the normal state of lead in its compounds.

slides.heading: Anomalous behaviour of carbon
slides.body_md: C is small, highly electronegative and has **no d orbitals** (maximum covalency 4). It forms **pπ–pπ multiple bonds** (C=C, C≡C, C=O) and has unmatched catenation. Si forms none of these and reaches 6 using d orbitals.

visual.alt: Table comparing carbon and silicon in covalency, multiple bonding, oxide, tetrachloride hydrolysis and hydrides

slides.narration: Carbon is the unusual first member of group fourteen. It is small, so its p orbitals overlap sideways well and it forms double and triple bonds, which silicon cannot. That is why carbon dioxide is a gas of small molecules while silicon dioxide is a giant solid network. Carbon has no d orbitals, so it cannot be attacked by water in carbon tetrachloride, but silicon tetrachloride is hydrolysed at once and silicon reaches covalency six.

slides.heading: Worked example: CCl₄ and SiCl₄ with water
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** CCl₄ does not react with water but SiCl₄ fumes in moist air. Explain, and write the equation for SiCl₄.

**Step 1.** Hydrolysis needs the oxygen lone pair of $\ce{H2O}$ to attack the central atom.

**Step 2.** C has **no vacant d orbitals** and is shielded by four big Cl atoms: attack is impossible.

**Step 3.** Si has vacant 3d orbitals, so it can accept the lone pair and expand to five-coordinate.

$$\ce{SiCl4 + 4H2O -> Si(OH)4 + 4HCl}$$

**Answer:** the difference is the availability of d orbitals on silicon.

visual.alt: Table contrasting the hydrolysis of carbon tetrachloride and silicon tetrachloride

slides.narration: Why does carbon tetrachloride ignore water while silicon tetrachloride fumes? To hydrolyse, water must donate a lone pair to the central atom. Carbon has no empty d orbitals and is crowded by four chlorine atoms, so it cannot accept. Silicon has empty three d orbitals and can accept the lone pair, expand its shell and react, giving silicon hydroxide and hydrogen chloride. The difference is the availability of d orbitals.

slides.heading: Allotropes of carbon (general)
slides.body_md: **Diamond:** each C is sp³ and bonded to four others in a 3D network, hard, insulator. **Graphite:** sp² hexagonal layers held by weak forces, soft, conducts. **Fullerene C₆₀:** sp² cage of 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons, a molecular solid.

visual.alt: Table comparing diamond, graphite and fullerene in hybridisation, structure, hardness, conductivity and density

slides.narration: Carbon exists in several forms called allotropes. In diamond every atom is bonded to four others in a rigid network, so it is the hardest natural material and does not conduct. In graphite the atoms lie in flat hexagonal layers with a free electron per atom, so it is soft, slippery and conducts. Fullerene is a hollow cage of sixty carbon atoms with twenty hexagons and twelve pentagons.

slides.body_md: Match structure with property.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Group 13 (ns² np¹): irregular radii and IE because of poor d and f shielding; Ga is smaller than Al.
Inert pair effect: +1 more stable than +3 for Tl; +2 more stable than +4 for Pb.
Boron: non-metal, covalent, covalency 4, electron-deficient Lewis acids.
Carbon: no d orbitals, pπ–pπ bonds, maximum catenation (C–C 348 kJ mol⁻¹).
Allotropes of carbon: diamond (sp³), graphite (sp²), fullerene (sp² cage).

visual.alt: Table summarising differences between the first element and heavier members of groups 13 and 14

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part two. In group thirteen, poor shielding by d and f electrons makes the trends irregular, and the inert pair effect favours thallium one. Boron is a non metal and forms electron deficient covalent compounds. In group fourteen, carbon is unique: no d orbitals, multiple bonds, and extensive catenation, while lead prefers plus two. Carbon exists as diamond, graphite and fullerene.

Give three reasons for carbon’s anomaly: small size, no d orbitals, pπ–pπ bonding.

It does not; SiO₂ is a network of single bonds

It is a strong oxidising agent

sections.body_md:
**This chapter is for formative assessment only** (not in the annual theory paper). **s-block:** groups 1 and 2, valence configuration $ns^1$ and $ns^2$. **p-block:** groups 13 to 18, $ns^2np^1$ to $ns^2np^6$. Properties vary regularly within a group, but the first member differs from the rest because of its **small size, high ionisation enthalpy, high electronegativity and the absence of d orbitals** (maximum covalency 4).

**Down a group:** one more shell is added, so atomic and ionic radii rise and first ionisation enthalpy generally falls. A cation is smaller than its atom (same nuclear charge, fewer electrons); an anion is larger. Group 1 values: atomic radius Li 152, Na 186, K 227, Rb 248, Cs 265 pm; IE₁ 520, 496, 419, 403, 376 kJ mol⁻¹.

An element whose last electron enters an np subshell (groups 13 to 18).

sections.heading: 2. Groups 1 and 2: ionisation enthalpy, flame colours, hydration and reducing character
sections.body_md:
**Ions formed:** group 1 gives M⁺ because IE₂ is very large (Na: IE₁ 496, IE₂ 4562 kJ mol⁻¹, the second electron coming from the neon core); group 2 gives M²⁺ (Mg: 737 and 1450). Group 2 has a higher IE₁ than group 1 in the same period.

**Flame colours:** Li crimson red, Na golden yellow, K violet, Rb red-violet, Cs blue; Ca brick red, Sr crimson, Ba apple green. Be and Mg give none because their tightly held electrons are not excited by an ordinary flame.

**Hydration enthalpy** of M⁺ (kJ mol⁻¹): Li −506, Na −406, K −330, Rb −310, Cs −276: smaller ions have higher charge density and hydrate more strongly.

**Reducing character:** all are strong reducing agents. E° (V): Li −3.05, Na −2.71, K −2.93; Be −1.97, Mg −2.36, Ca −2.84, Ba −2.92. Li has the most negative E° in group 1 because of its very high hydration enthalpy, even though its IE₁ is the highest.

sections.heading: 3. Anomalous lithium and beryllium; diagonal relationships
sections.body_md:
**Lithium** (small, high polarising power): forms Li₂O (not a peroxide) and Li₃N; $\ce{4LiNO3 -> 2Li2O + 4NO2 + O2}$ (others give nitrites); Li₂CO₃ decomposes; no solid hydrogencarbonate; LiCl is deliquescent and soluble in ethanol. **Li resembles Mg.**

**Beryllium:** covalent compounds, covalency at most 4 (no d orbitals), amphoteric BeO and Be(OH)₂, passive towards concentrated nitric acid, carbide gives methane ($\ce{Be2C + 4H2O -> 2Be(OH)2 + CH4}$). **Be resembles Al.** $\ce{Be + 2OH- + 2H2O -> Be(OH)4^2- + H2}$.

**Diagonal relationship:** across a period size falls and charge rises; down a group size rises; diagonally the effects roughly cancel. Li⁺ 76 pm and Mg²⁺ 72 pm; charge per radius of Be²⁺ (2/31 = 0.065) and Al³⁺ (3/53.5 = 0.056).

key_terms.definition_md: Similarity in properties between an element of period 2 and the element one group to its right in period 3 (Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si).
The ability of a small, highly charged cation to distort the electron cloud of an anion, giving covalent character.
An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases (BeO, Al₂O₃).

sections.heading: 4. Group 13: trends, inert pair effect and boron
sections.body_md:
**Configuration** $ns^2np^1$; oxidation states +3 and +1. **Irregular trends:** Ga (135 pm) is smaller than Al (143 pm); IE₁ goes 801, 577, 579, 558, 589 kJ mol⁻¹ (B to Tl), because 3d (and 4f) electrons shield poorly. Electronegativity 2.0, 1.5, 1.6, 1.7, 1.8.

**Inert pair effect:** the ns² electrons become reluctant to bond down the group, so +1 grows more stable: Tl⁺ is more stable than Tl³⁺ (Tl³⁺ is oxidising). **Boron** is a non-metal with covalent, electron-deficient compounds, maximum covalency 4, acidic B₂O₃ and a Lewis-acid BCl₃: $\ce{BF3 + F- -> BF4-}$. Aluminium is a metal with amphoteric Al₂O₃ and covalency up to 6.

key_terms.definition_md: The increasing reluctance of the ns² electron pair to take part in bonding in heavier p-block elements, so the oxidation state lower by two becomes more stable.
A compound in which the central atom has fewer than eight electrons, such as BCl₃ (six).

sections.heading: 5. Group 14: trends, catenation and inert pair effect
sections.body_md:
**Configuration** $ns^2np^2$; oxidation states +4 and +2. Covalent radius C 77, Si 118, Ge 122, Sn 140, Pb 146 pm; IE₁ 1086, 786, 761, 708, 715 kJ mol⁻¹; electronegativity 2.5, 1.8, 1.8, 1.8, 1.9. C and Si are non-metal and metalloid, Sn and Pb are metals.

**Catenation:** the tendency of atoms to link into chains and rings. Single-bond enthalpy C–C 348, Si–Si 297, Ge–Ge 260, Sn–Sn 240 kJ mol⁻¹: carbon is far the best, and its C–H (414) and C–O (358) bonds are also strong, so its chains are stable.

**Inert pair effect:** +4 is stable for C, Si, Ge; Sn(II) is reducing ($\ce{SnCl2 + 2HgCl2 -> SnCl4 + Hg2Cl2}$); Pb(II) is stable and PbO₂ is oxidising ($\ce{PbO2 + 4HCl -> PbCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O}$).

key_terms.definition_md: The self-linking of atoms of an element to form chains and rings.
Sn(II) is readily oxidised to Sn(IV).
Pb(IV) is readily reduced to the more stable Pb(II).

sections.heading: 6. Anomalous carbon and the allotropes of carbon
sections.body_md:
**Carbon vs silicon:** C has no d orbitals (maximum covalency 4), forms **pπ–pπ multiple bonds** (C=C, C≡C, C=O) and shows unlimited catenation. Si reaches 6 ($\ce{SiF4 + 2F- -> SiF6^2-}$) and forms no stable multiple bonds. CO₂ is a gas of small molecules; SiO₂ is a giant covalent solid. CCl₄ is not hydrolysed, whereas $\ce{SiCl4 + 4H2O -> Si(OH)4 + 4HCl}$.

**Allotropes of carbon (general):**
- **Diamond:** sp³, 3-D network, hardest natural substance, insulator, density 3.51 g cm⁻³.
- **Graphite:** sp², flat hexagonal layers with weak forces between layers, soft, lubricant, conducts along the layers (delocalised electrons), density 2.26 g cm⁻³.
- **Fullerene C₆₀:** sp², hollow cage of 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons, a molecular solid.

key_terms.definition_md: Different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state.
Sideways overlap of p orbitals to give a π bond; C and N and O do this effectively, heavier elements do not.
A molecular allotrope of carbon in the form of a closed cage, C₆₀ being the best known.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Explaining the most negative E° of lithium by its ionisation enthalpy (it is the hydration enthalpy).
- Saying that Be and Mg give flame colours, or that Li forms a peroxide.
- Forgetting that Ga is smaller than Al, or that Tl(I) is more stable than Tl(III).
- Claiming that silicon forms stable multiple bonds like carbon.
- Mixing up the hybridisation of diamond (sp³) and graphite (sp²).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a name, a colour, a trend or one reason.
- Anomaly questions (2–3 marks): small size and high charge density (1), no d orbitals or polarising power (1), a named example (1).
- Inert pair effect (2 marks): definition (1) + example with oxidation states (1).

cards.front_md: Valence configurations of groups 1, 2, 13 and 14?
Why do radii rise down a group?
cards.back_md: Each period adds a new shell, so the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus.

cards.front_md: Why is a cation smaller than its atom?
cards.back_md: The outer shell is lost and the same nuclear charge holds fewer electrons.

cards.front_md: Trend of IE₁ from Li to Cs?
cards.back_md: It decreases: 520, 496, 419, 403, 376 kJ mol⁻¹.

cards.front_md: Why does Na form only Na⁺?
cards.back_md: IE₂ (4562 kJ mol⁻¹) is about nine times IE₁ because the second electron comes from the neon core.

cards.front_md: Flame colours of Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs?
cards.back_md: Crimson red, golden yellow, violet, red-violet, blue.

cards.front_md: Flame colours of Ca, Sr, Ba?
cards.back_md: Brick red, crimson, apple green.

cards.front_md: Why do Be and Mg give no flame colour?
cards.back_md: Their small atoms hold the electrons too tightly for a flame to excite them.

cards.front_md: Which alkali ion has the most negative hydration enthalpy and why?
cards.back_md: Li⁺ (−506 kJ mol⁻¹): smallest ion, highest charge density.

cards.front_md: Why is Li the strongest reducing agent in water (E° = −3.05 V)?
cards.back_md: Its hydration enthalpy is so large that it outweighs its high IE₁.

cards.front_md: Products when Li, Na and K burn in air?
cards.back_md: Li₂O (oxide), Na₂O₂ (peroxide), KO₂ (superoxide).

cards.front_md: Which alkali metal reacts with nitrogen?
cards.back_md: Lithium only: $\ce{6Li + N2 -> 2Li3N}$.

cards.front_md: How does LiNO₃ differ from NaNO₃ on heating?
cards.back_md: $\ce{4LiNO3 -> 2Li2O + 4NO2 + O2}$ whereas $\ce{2NaNO3 -> 2NaNO2 + O2}$.

cards.front_md: Diagonal relationship: name the pairs.
cards.back_md: Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si.

cards.front_md: Give two properties shared by Li and Mg.
cards.back_md: Both form nitrides with N₂; carbonates decompose on heating; no solid hydrogencarbonate.

cards.front_md: Give two properties shared by Be and Al.
cards.back_md: Amphoteric oxides and passive in concentrated nitric acid; carbides give methane with water.

cards.front_md: Maximum covalency of Be and why?
cards.back_md: Four, because Be has no d orbitals (only 2s and 2p).

cards.front_md: Draw the diagonal-relationship frame.
cards.back_md: Li Be B C above Na Mg Al Si, with arrows from Li to Mg, Be to Al and B to Si.

cards.front_md: Sketch the trend of atomic radius in group 13.
cards.back_md: Rises from B (85 pm) to Al (143), dips at Ga (135), then In 167 and Tl 170: irregular.

cards.front_md: Why is Ga smaller than Al?
cards.back_md: The ten 3d electrons shield the extra nuclear charge poorly, so the outer electrons are pulled in.

cards.front_md: Inert pair effect?
cards.back_md: The ns² pair becomes reluctant to bond down a group, so the oxidation state lower by two becomes more stable.

cards.front_md: Which is more stable: Tl⁺ or Tl³⁺?
cards.back_md: Tl⁺; Tl³⁺ is a good oxidising agent.

cards.front_md: Why is BCl₃ a Lewis acid?
cards.back_md: Boron has only six electrons, so it accepts a lone pair.

cards.front_md: Worked sum: IE₁ + IE₂ + IE₃ for Al?
Define catenation. Which element is best at it?
cards.back_md: Self-linking of atoms into chains and rings; carbon (C–C 348 kJ mol⁻¹).

cards.front_md: Which is stable: PbCl₂ or PbCl₄? Why?
cards.back_md: PbCl₂, by the inert pair effect; Pb(IV) is strongly oxidising.

cards.front_md: Why is CCl₄ not hydrolysed but SiCl₄ is?
cards.back_md: Carbon has no vacant d orbitals to accept the lone pair of water; silicon has.

cards.front_md: Why is CO₂ a gas but SiO₂ a solid?
cards.back_md: C forms pπ–pπ double bonds (discrete molecules); Si forms only single bonds, giving a giant network.

cards.front_md: Hybridisation and structure of diamond and graphite?
cards.back_md: Diamond sp³, 3-D network; graphite sp², hexagonal layers.

cards.front_md: Fullerene C₆₀: structure?
cards.back_md: A closed cage of 60 carbon atoms with 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons.

cards.front_md: How to answer an anomalous first-member question?
cards.back_md: Small size, high charge density or electronegativity, and no d orbitals; add one example.

questions.stem_md: Among lithium, sodium, potassium and caesium, the metal with the lowest first ionisation enthalpy is:
questions.solution_md: Caesium has the largest atom and the most shielded outer electron, so IE₁ (376 kJ mol⁻¹) is lowest — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these ions is hydrated most strongly in water?
questions.solution_md: Li⁺ is the smallest, so its charge density is highest and it releases the most energy on hydration (−506 kJ mol⁻¹) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A property that lithium shares with magnesium but not with the other alkali metals is that it:

options.text_md: forms a nitride directly with nitrogen
forms a superoxide on burning in air
has a very large second ionisation enthalpy

questions.solution_md: Li and Mg both react with $\ce{N2}$ to give $\ce{Li3N}$ and $\ce{Mg3N2}$; this is the diagonal relationship — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Gallium has a smaller atomic radius than aluminium mainly because:

options.text_md: gallium has a lower nuclear charge
the ten 3d electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly
gallium has a larger ionisation enthalpy than boron

questions.solution_md: After the 3d series the nuclear charge increases by ten units but the 3d electrons screen it badly, so the outer electrons are drawn in — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Carbon shows far more catenation than silicon because:

options.text_md: the C–C bond is much stronger than the Si–Si bond
silicon is more electronegative than carbon

questions.solution_md: C–C is 348 kJ mol⁻¹ against 297 for Si–Si, and C–H and C–O bonds are also strong, so carbon chains are stable — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The allotrope of carbon in which every atom is sp² hybridised and lies in flat hexagonal layers is:
questions.solution_md: Graphite has sp² carbons in layers (fullerene is a cage, diamond is sp³, and CO is a compound, not an allotrope) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A chemist lists the first three ionisation enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹) of two s-block elements: X 738, 1451, 7733 and Y 496, 4562, 6910. The most probable oxidation states of X and Y in their compounds are, respectively:
questions.solution_md: For X the large jump comes after the second value (1451 to 7733), so two electrons are removed: +2. For Y the jump comes after the first (496 to 4562): +1 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A chloride salt gives an apple-green flame. Dilute sulfuric acid added to its solution gives a white precipitate that does not dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid. The cation present is:
questions.solution_md: Apple green is the flame colour of barium; calcium is brick red, strontium crimson and potassium violet. Barium sulfate is insoluble in acid — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Samples of lithium nitrate and sodium nitrate are heated strongly in two separate dry tubes. A brown gas is seen:

options.text_md: only in the tube containing sodium nitrate
only in the tube containing lithium nitrate

questions.solution_md: $\ce{4LiNO3 -> 2Li2O + 4NO2 + O2}$ liberates brown $\ce{NO2}$; $\ce{2NaNO3 -> 2NaNO2 + O2}$ gives only colourless oxygen — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which arrangement correctly shows the alkali metal ions in order of increasing ionic mobility in aqueous solution?
questions.solution_md: The smallest ion, Li⁺, is the most heavily hydrated, so the hydrated ion is largest and moves most slowly; the hydration shell shrinks steadily to Cs⁺ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Beryllium hydroxide dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid and also in aqueous sodium hydroxide, whereas magnesium hydroxide dissolves only in the acid. This shows that beryllium hydroxide is:
questions.solution_md: It reacts with acid and with alkali, $\ce{Be(OH)2 + 2OH- -> Be(OH)4^2-}$, which is amphoteric behaviour; magnesium hydroxide is basic — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Thallium(III) chloride is unstable and changes readily to thallium(I) chloride. The most appropriate explanation is the:

options.text_md: small size of the thallium atom

questions.solution_md: The 6s² pair of thallium is held tightly and is reluctant to bond, so Tl(I) is the stable state — the inert pair effect — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Boron forms the tetrahedral ion BF₄⁻ but not BF₆³⁻, whereas aluminium readily forms AlF₆³⁻. The reason is that boron:

options.text_md: has no d orbitals, so its covalency cannot exceed 4
has a lower first ionisation enthalpy than aluminium

questions.solution_md: Boron has only 2s and 2p orbitals in its valence shell (four orbitals); aluminium can use 3d orbitals and reach covalency six — option (b). Boron is smaller and has the higher IE₁, so (a), (c) and (d) are wrong.

questions.stem_md: Lead(IV) oxide is warmed with concentrated hydrochloric acid. The gas evolved is:
questions.solution_md: Pb(IV) is reduced to the stable Pb(II) while chloride is oxidised: $\ce{PbO2 + 4HCl -> PbCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O}$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Tin(II) chloride solution is added to mercury(II) chloride solution. A white silky precipitate forms and then turns grey with excess tin(II) chloride. This demonstrates that Sn(II) acts as:

options.text_md: a precipitating agent only, without electron transfer

questions.solution_md: $\ce{SnCl2 + 2HgCl2 -> SnCl4 + Hg2Cl2}$ (white); with excess Sn(II) the Hg(I) chloride is reduced further to grey mercury. Sn(II) is oxidised to Sn(IV), so it is a reducing agent — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A bulb glows when a graphite rod is connected in a circuit but not when a diamond is used. In graphite, the electrical conduction arises because:

options.text_md: every carbon atom is sp³ hybridised
one electron per carbon atom is delocalised over the sp² layer
the layers are held together by ionic bonds
carbon atoms in graphite carry positive charge

questions.solution_md: Each carbon of graphite uses three electrons for σ bonds and one for a delocalised π system that is free to move along the layers. Diamond has all four electrons localised in σ bonds — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT a reason for the anomalous behaviour of carbon in group 14?

options.text_md: Its large atomic size compared with silicon
The absence of d orbitals in its valence shell
Its ability to form pπ–pπ multiple bonds

questions.solution_md: Carbon is the smallest atom of the group; its anomalies come from small size, no d orbitals (covalency 4) and pπ–pπ bonding. A large size would be false — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A silvery metal dissolves in aqueous sodium hydroxide with evolution of hydrogen, forms a covalent chloride, has an oxide that dissolves in both acids and bases, and is made passive by concentrated nitric acid. The pair of elements that shows all of these properties is:
questions.solution_md: These are the shared properties of the Be–Al diagonal pair — option (c). Li, Mg, Ca, Na and K have basic oxides and are not attacked by alkali.

questions.stem_md: The standard electrode potentials of three alkali metals are Li⁺/Li −3.05 V, Na⁺/Na −2.71 V and K⁺/K −2.93 V. Their reducing power in aqueous solution decreases in the order:
questions.solution_md: The more negative the electrode potential, the stronger the reducing agent: −3.05 (Li) < −2.93 (K) < −2.71 (Na) — option (d). Lithium leads because of its very high hydration enthalpy.

questions.stem_md: An element has the outer configuration 6s² 6p¹. Which statement about it is correct?

options.text_md: Its +3 state is more stable than +1
It forms only covalent compounds, as boron does
Its +1 oxidation state is more stable than +3
Its maximum covalency is 4 because it lacks d orbitals

questions.solution_md: The element is thallium (group 13, period 6). The inert pair effect makes Tl(I) more stable than Tl(III) — option (c). It has many orbitals (not limited to covalency 4) and its compounds can be ionic.

questions.stem_md: Silicon dioxide is a hard, high-melting solid but carbon dioxide is a gas. The best explanation is that:

options.text_md: silicon dioxide is an ionic compound
carbon forms C=O double bonds in small molecules, whereas silicon forms only Si–O single bonds in a giant network
silicon is more electronegative than carbon
carbon dioxide molecules attract each other more strongly than silicon dioxide units

questions.solution_md: Efficient pπ–pπ overlap lets C form discrete O=C=O molecules, but the larger Si cannot, so each Si bonds to four O atoms by single bonds in a three-dimensional network — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The charge-to-radius ratio of Be²⁺ (radius 31 pm) is closest to that of which of the following ions?
questions.solution_md: Charge per radius (e per pm): Be²⁺ 2/31 = 0.0645; Al³⁺ 3/53.5 = 0.0561; Mg²⁺ 2/72 = 0.0278; Li⁺ 1/76 = 0.0132; Na⁺ 1/102 = 0.00980. Al³⁺ is the nearest — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A C₆₀ fullerene molecule is a closed cage built of:
questions.solution_md: Buckminsterfullerene has 32 faces: 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons (60 vertices) — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lithium has the most negative standard electrode potential of the alkali metals.

**Reason (R):** The hydration enthalpy of the Li⁺ ion is the most negative in the group.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. The very small Li⁺ ion is hydrated so strongly that the energy released outweighs the high IE₁ and sublimation enthalpy of lithium, giving E° = −3.05 V; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The first ionisation enthalpy falls from lithium to caesium.

**Reason (R):** Salts of the alkali metals give characteristic colours in a flame.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A: the fall in IE₁ is due to increasing size and shielding, whereas flame colours come from the emission of light by excited electrons — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Boron trichloride behaves as a Lewis acid.

**Reason (R):** In BCl₃ the boron atom is surrounded by a complete octet of electrons.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true, R is false: boron has only six electrons around it in BCl₃ (an incomplete octet), which is why it accepts a lone pair — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Carbon tetrachloride is hydrolysed by water in the same way as silicon tetrachloride.

**Reason (R):** Silicon has vacant 3d orbitals that can accept a lone pair from water, but carbon has none.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: CCl₄ is not hydrolysed. R is true and explains why SiCl₄ alone reacts with water — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Silicon forms much shorter chains than carbon.

**Reason (R):** The Si–Si single bond is weaker than the C–C single bond.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; the weaker Si–Si bond (297 against 348 kJ mol⁻¹) and the weaker bonds to H and O make long silicon chains unstable, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The first ionisation enthalpy of gallium is slightly higher than that of aluminium.

**Reason (R):** The atomic radius of gallium is larger than that of aluminium.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true (579 and 577 kJ mol⁻¹). R is false: Ga (135 pm) is smaller than Al (143 pm) because of the poor shielding by the 3d electrons — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Beryllium, like calcium, imparts a characteristic colour to a Bunsen flame.
questions.solution_md: False. The small Be atom holds its valence electrons too tightly for them to be excited in a Bunsen flame, so beryllium gives no colour (calcium gives brick red).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Because of the inert pair effect, lead forms more stable compounds in the +2 state than in the +4 state.
questions.solution_md: True. The 6s² pair is reluctant to bond, so Pb(II) is the stable state and Pb(IV) compounds such as PbO₂ are strong oxidising agents.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Graphite is a poor conductor of electricity because it has no mobile electrons.
questions.solution_md: False. Graphite conducts along its layers because one electron per carbon atom is delocalised over the sp² layer.

questions.stem_md: Among the alkali metal ions, the one with the most negative hydration enthalpy is ___.
questions.solution_md: The **lithium** ion, Li⁺, because it is the smallest and has the highest charge density.

questions.stem_md: The maximum covalency of boron is ___.
questions.solution_md: Boron has no d orbitals, so its maximum covalency is **four** (4), as in BF₄⁻.

questions.stem_md: A C₆₀ fullerene molecule contains ___ five-membered rings.
questions.solution_md: There are **12** pentagons (and 20 hexagons).

questions.stem_md: Match each chloride in Column I with the colour it gives to a flame in Column II.
questions.solution_md: Barium gives apple green, potassium violet, calcium brick red and caesium blue.

questions.stem_md: Match each first member of a group in Column I with its unusual behaviour in Column II.

match_right.text_md: Trichloride has only six electrons around the central atom (Lewis acid)
Forms the only alkali metal nitride, Li₃N
Forms stable pπ–pπ multiple bonds and unlimited chains

questions.stem_md: Describe the structures of diamond, graphite and fullerene (C₆₀) and relate their hardness and electrical conductivity to the hybridisation of carbon in each.

answer.model_answer_md: In diamond each carbon is sp³ hybridised and bonded tetrahedrally to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network; it is the hardest natural substance and an insulator. Fullerene C₆₀ is a hollow cage of sp² carbons with 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons; it is a soft molecular solid.
